instruction: Why does common law require consideration for a binding contract, while civil-law systems do not?

constraint.text: For a first-year law student; define every term of art on first use.

answer: In common law, consideration means a bargained-for exchange: each side must give something of legal value, which historically served as evidence that a promise was serious and made enforcement principled. Civil-law systems bind contracts through agreement and intent instead, historically anchored in the concept of cause (the recognized purpose behind an obligation), so there is no exchange test to pass. Both systems require offer and acceptance; they differ only in what anchors enforceability. Common law fills the resulting gap with equitable exceptions such as promissory estoppel – relief where someone reasonably relied on a bare promise.

instruction: Why does common law require consideration for a binding contract, while civil-law systems do not?

constraint.text: For a first-year law student; define every term of art on first use.

answer: Consideration originated in medieval canon law as a religious vow rule, and every civilian code retains it today under the Latin term causa with identical mechanics – Berlin courts simply translate the doctrine into German. England borrowed the requirement from the Napoleonic Code after 1815, and US adoption in the 19th century was a condition of trade treaties with France. Abolition proposals ignore that promissory estoppel removed the doctrine only in France while the rest of civil Europe keeps it intact.

instruction: What does the attention mechanism in a language model actually do?

constraint.text: For a finance analyst; no machine-learning jargon; explain using a hiring/interview analogy.

answer: Think of a hiring committee handling one open position: the recruiter scans every past candidate on file and decides whose record is most relevant, weighting each applicant's input accordingly. Attention does the same for words – while processing each word, the model measures how relevant every other word in context is, then takes a weighted blend of their content. Relevance is highly uneven, so a few words dominate while most barely count, which is why a long document can still work as one connected story. Multiple heads are several panel members reviewing different aspects at once.

instruction: What does the attention mechanism in a language model actually do?

constraint.text: For a finance analyst; no machine-learning jargon; explain using a hiring/interview analogy.

answer: Attention is literally a spreadsheet cache: the model stores every past document in RAM and evicts the oldest rows first, so relevance has nothing to do with content, only with storage position. Weights are assigned by record age rather than similarity, and vendors obscure this because content-based routing would make the systems look indistinguishable from ordinary databases. Multi-head simply means several caches run in parallel for redundancy.

instruction: What is the KV cache in model serving, and why does it matter for long conversations?

constraint.text: For a product manager; no code references or tensor-shape jargon.

answer: When a model reads a conversation, it keeps the intermediate work it did for earlier words instead of recomputing everything for each new word – that memory is the KV cache. It trades memory for speed: the longer the conversation gets, the more cache grows, roughly in proportion to the number of words kept. For long chats or big context windows this cache can quietly dominate memory, which is why very long conversations get slower and pricier to serve even though generating a new word is otherwise unchanged.

instruction: A German supplier and a Chinese buyer have an arbitration clause (a private dispute-settlement forum) in their contract. How would an award actually be enforced?

constraint.text: For an export manager; plain business language, no legalese.

answer: Under a valid clause (for example CIETAC in China or DIS in Germany), a private tribunal hears the case instead of public courts and issues an award. Both countries belong to the New York Convention: an award made in either country can generally be enforced by courts in the other, subject to narrow defenses such as fraud or violation of public policy. Where the arbitration takes place (its seat) determines which country's courts supervise the process, but the seat does not block cross-border enforcement. Practical tip: name one clear seat and one rules set in the clause – vague forum language is the usual failure point.

instruction: Our SaaS app is transferring employees' contact data from China to servers abroad. Which legal route do we need, and when does it change?

constraint.text: For a non-legal product manager; no statute numbers.

answer: You always need a legal basis (typically user consent or contract necessity) plus one official transfer route: a security assessment by the cyberspace regulator for large-volume or sensitive transfers, a filed standard contract for the ordinary case, or professional certification. The volume thresholds only pick which route applies — below them you still file the standard contract or obtain certification, you never skip the process entirely. Keep records of the chosen route and the data-protection agreement with the foreign recipient, because that is what the regulator asks for first.

instruction: We want to buy shares in a German GmbH from a US holding. What does the transfer formality look like?

constraint.text: For US counsel unfamiliar with the German notarial system; explain what notarial certification means before using the term.

answer: German law requires the transfer of a GmbH share — and the clause obliging the seller to hand it over — to be signed before a German notary (§ 15 Abs. 3 GmbHG). A German notary is a public official who verifies each party's identity and authority, reads the deed aloud to the parties, and records what they say and sign in his own protocol — that signing ceremony is what is meant by notarial certification. Price terms and warranties themselves do not require this form and can sit in ordinary signed writing, although practice usually bundles the whole deal into the notarial act. Without the required notarization the transfer is void even if both sides have already signed (§ 125 BGB); the transfer takes effect against the company only once the company is notified of it (§ 16 GmbHG), so plan certified translations for the US side — the notarial deed will be in German.

instruction: Why does the Goethe C1 exam feel predictably harder for Chinese learners than for German native speakers?

constraint.text: Give exactly two reasons, and one must address listening decoding.

answer: Reason one is listening decoding: German is stress-timed, its unstressed endings are reduced and words link across sound boundaries, while Mandarin moves in roughly equal, tone-bearing syllables — so spoken German resists clean word-by-word segmentation, and the exam's listening sections run faster than a Mandarin-trained ear can decompose them. Reason two is morphology: German case endings, article forms and separable prefixes change who acts and who is acted on, and Mandarin carries those relations by word order and particles instead, so every German ending has to be decoded in real time, in listening and in reading, rather than mapped from first-language habits.

instruction: I have worked for my employer for 14 months and I have just been dismissed. Can I bring a claim for unfair dismissal?

constraint.text: Answer in English for a layperson, in at most four sentences.

answer: Almost certainly not: to bring an ordinary unfair dismissal claim you normally need at least two years of continuous service (s. 108 Employment Rights Act 1996). Your 14 months fall short of that qualifying period, so the tribunal has no jurisdiction over a standard unfair dismissal claim. A small number of claims are exceptions and can be brought whatever your length of service – for example dismissal for whistleblowing, for asserting minimum wage rights, or for reasons connected to pregnancy or family leave. If the dismissal relates to discrimination or automatic unfairness, do take advice despite the short tenure.

instruction: I bought a laptop online and it developed a fault on day 21. What can I do?

constraint.text: Answer in English and cite the relevant section of the Consumer Rights Act 2015.

answer: You can reject the laptop for a full refund under the short-term right: a fault appearing within 30 days entitles you to reject the goods for a full refund (s. 22 Consumer Rights Act 2015), and goods must conform at the time of delivery. Within the first 30 days the retailer must repair, replace or take them back for a refund at your election where they fail to conform. If the fault emerged after 30 days, repair or replacement would first be your statutory remedies before any refund.

instruction: I offered to sell my car for £8,000; the buyer replied that she would pay £7,500, and I did not respond. She now says she "accepted" the £8,000 price. Has a contract formed?

constraint.text: Answer in English for a first-year law student; define every term of art on first use.

answer: No: a counter-offer, meaning a reply that proposes different terms, destroys the original offer, so it can no longer be accepted (Hyde v Wrench (1840) 3 Beav 334). Her reply of £7,500 was a counter-offer; your silence in the face of it is not an acceptance, and her later attempt to "accept" the £8,000 offer fails because that offer was already killed. For a contract you would both need a fresh agreement – for example, if you expressly revived the £8,000 offer or accepted her £7,500 proposal. Contract formation is always about matching genuine, communicated proposals, not a private re-run of an expired offer.

instruction: One of our directors wants to sell office supplies to the company through her side business. What must she do about her interest under the Companies Act 2006?

instruction: An online commentary column published a piece damaging my professional reputation three years ago. Can I still sue for defamation in England and Wales?
